chapter: Piano influences: Teddy Wilson, Tatum and Bud Powell
title: Meeting Art Tatum through Booker Coleman and his mother
summary: Tatum stays at Mrs. Coleman's house, listens kindly to every pianist, and Malachi spends days and nights playing with him.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Art Tatum: the legend, the piano and the man

blocks.x: But this was, I guess, around in the late Thirties. Then around 1941 (I think it was '41, or it might have been '40, somewhere between '41 and '40), I had the extreme pleasure -- it was like a dream come true -- to meet Art Tatum. It so happens that a fellow that I mentioned before that had a band, Booker Coleman, had been friends with Art Tatum for years. He had known him since he was a very young man, so much to the extent that Art always called Booker's mother...he called her "Mama" too. And there were so many incidents where I would be at Mrs. Coleman's house... Art used to stay there a lot when he came to Washington. And Booker and Art would get to arguing about anything. Sometimes they were arguing about playing the piano. One wanted the other one to get up. And it was kind of funny to hear two grown men holler upstairs for Mrs. Coleman: "Mama, Art's doing this or that!" And these were grown guys; it was more less funny.

Art Tatum. Just meeting him and learning so much from him... Because he was a guy that just loved all pianists. No matter how little you played, he always had a listening ear for you. I just stuck to Art Tatum like glue. Whenever he

came to town... I remember at times telling my wife that Art Tatum just came in town and he's around at Booker's house, and they had called me. She said, 'Well, okay, I'll see you in a couple of days.' Because that meant I was going to be with Art Tatum all day, or I would go to work with him, then after we would hang out and we would drink and play all night at somebody's house, and everybody would fall asleep on the couch or something, and other pianists would play. There was always at least, oh, eight or ten pianists around. Everybody was playing. And Art would play until he got tired, and he'd probably fall on the couch and go to sleep.
In hanging out with him like that, it was always a learning thing. It was like being in school.
